original_question: For equivariant map algebras whose target algebra is not the finite-dimensional Lie or associative algebra considered in the standard theory, develop the representation theory of the resulting EMA. In particular, determine finite-dimensional representations when the target is a Kac-Moody algebra, the Heisenberg algebra, an alternative algebra, a Jordan algebra, or another algebra with a well-defined notion of representation.
target_in_paper: Section 4.1(b), "More general targets," in the open problems section. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s target open problem as the study of EMAs with target algebras beyond the finite-dimensional Lie and associative cases emphasized earlier in the survey, and it reproduces the paper’s concrete examples: Kac-Moody algebras, the Heisenberg algebra, and algebras with well-defined representations such as alternative and Jordan algebras. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))
missing_details: The paper’s ambient setup is still an equivariant map algebra built from an affine scheme X = Spec A over an algebraically closed field k, together with a finite group Γ acting by automorphisms on A and on the target algebra; your draft does not state this data. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))

To be stand-alone, the EMA should be defined algebraically as M(X, a)^Γ := (a ⊗ A)^Γ, using the induced Γ-action on a ⊗ A; this is especially important here because the target a may be infinite-dimensional, so the regular-map interpretation is no longer the safest formulation. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))

Section 4.1(b) varies the target algebra only; broadening Γ is a different open problem in Section 4.1(a). A paper-faithful reformulation should therefore keep the standard finite-group action unless it explicitly says otherwise. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))

The exact emphasis in the paper is split: for Kac-Moody and Heisenberg targets, the authors say one should study the resulting representation theory; for alternative and Jordan targets, they explicitly single out finite-dimensional representations. Your draft compresses these into a single uniform demand. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))

The contrast is not only with finite-dimensional targets: the paper also wants to move outside the Lie/associative categories themselves, to any class of target algebra having a well-defined notion of representation. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))

The paper notes one existing point of comparison, namely the untwisted multiloop Kac-Moody case [ERF], so the intended question is to extend EMA theory beyond that isolated example rather than to ignore prior work entirely. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))
refined_question: Let k be an algebraically closed field, let X = Spec A be an affine k-scheme, let Γ be a finite group acting by automorphisms on A and on a target algebra a, and define the equivariant map algebra by M(X, a)^Γ := (a ⊗ A)^Γ. Extend the representation-theoretic study of equivariant map algebras to the case of more general targets a—specifically when a is a Kac-Moody algebra or the Heisenberg algebra, and more generally when a is any algebra equipped with a standard notion of representation—and, in particular, determine the finite-dimensional representations when a is an alternative algebra or a Jordan algebra. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))
justification: The draft is aiming at the open problem in Section 4.1(b), not at the classification theorems in Sections 2 or 3. The introduction says Section 4.1 concerns “new types of EMAs,” and Section 4.1(b) then explicitly asks for EMAs with more general target algebras, naming Kac-Moody and Heisenberg Lie algebras and then widening the scope to any target algebra with well-defined representations, with finite-dimensional representations for alternative and Jordan algebras as the concrete example. Definitions 1.1 and 1.3, together with Remarks 1.2, supply the algebraic EMA framework needed to make the question stand alone in a way that remains faithful even when the target is no longer finite-dimensional. ([mysite.science.uottawa.ca](https://mysite.science.uottawa.ca/neher/Papers/2013EMA-survey.pdf))
